messages.author: e32484f448e128cc
messages.subject: centering AR model?
parts:
Hi list,
I would like to fit a model in which there're several layers of nesting. So say you have repeated data y[i,j,k] for occurrence i for individual j and for year k, ie there are several values y[1,j,k],...y[I_j,j,k] in each year (incidentally, these are Poisson counts, so the linear predictor is then defined on a log scale). The dataset is also balanced so for each j there are the same number of observations in every year k.

I would like to build a structure in which there's a year/individual-specific effect, which is centered around the pooled individual mean. Because of the time component, I'd like to model the year/individual effects using AR(1) model. I think the standard version of AR(p) in INLA is actually centered around 0 (in fact with a sum-to-zero constraint?), so what I'd like to do is to actually model something like
+...f(individual:year,model="ar",SOME_OPTIONS)
so that this is actually centered on 
f(individual,model="iid")

Is there an easy (and computationally clever) way of doing so? (Notice that there are other covariates in the linear predictor, including, for now, an overall intercept). To make it even more complex, there are in fact 2 such structures that I would need to build for every individual (based on different covariates/indices).

Does any of this make sense?
Thanks!
Gianluca

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] centering AR model?
parts:
Hi Gianluca,

I'm not sure I can answer your question completely, but maybe there's a PC prior for that :p

The AR(p) model in INLA is a proper Gaussian with zero mean, so it doesn't have any extra constraints.

Sigrunn wrote a really nice paper about using priors to centre an AR(p) model on an AR(p-1) model, which might answer your question.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.08941.pdf

I'm not sure if these are implemented in INLA (but they are for AR(1): inla.doc("pc.cor0")).

Best wishes,

Dan

parts:
On Mon, 2017-02-20 at 12:15 +0000, Daniel Simpson wrote:
> Hi Gianluca,
>
> I'm not sure I can answer your question completely, but maybe there's
> a PC prior for that :p
>
> The AR(p) model in INLA is a proper Gaussian with zero mean, so it
> doesn't have any extra constraints.
>
> Sigrunn wrote a really nice paper about using priors to centre an
> AR(p) model on an AR(p-1) model, which might answer your question.
> https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.08941.pdf
>
> I'm not sure if these are implemented in INLA (but they are for
> AR(1): inla.doc("pc.cor0")).

yes, you want the pc.cor0 prior, for the correlation to make it shrink
to the iid model. maybe also pc.prec prior for the precision to make it
shrink to a constant. the model="ar",order=p model has these priors as
default (as explained in the paper) but not the AR1 model.

as Dan says, there is no sum to zero constraint on these models unless
you ask for it yourself.

Best
H

On Monday, 20 February 2017 16:57:44 UTC, Finn Lindgren wrote:
I think it would help if you wrote the mathematical definition of the model you want. "Shrink towards" can have several different meanings.  What you wrote as desired inla f() call was, to me, an interaction model, and not a prior shrinkage model, so being more specific with the maths might clear things up!

Good point.

So, here's what I would like
y[i,j,k] ~ Poisson(theta[i,j,k])
log(theta[i,j,k]) = X*beta + gamma[j,k]
for (k=2:K)
  gamma[j,k] = delta[j] + phi[j]*gamma[j,k-1] + w[j,k]
  w[j,k] ~ Normal(0,t)
for (j in 1:J)
  delta[j] ~ Normal(0,sigma_delta)
sigma_delta ~ some model for the SD
beta ~Normal(0,v)

In the log-linear predictor there's an unstructured component with some coefficients beta and a matrix of covariates X. Then there's the structured effect gamma, which is specific to each individual j in each year k. What I would like is this structured effect to be centered around an individual-specific mean delta[j], so that I can get some sort of pooled estimate (delta) and a time-specific estimate (gamma), for each individual.

Does this make sense?
Gianluca

Finn
